name: Bramble
lede: Bramble is a dark, purple-tinged near-black named for the blackberry bush; the books know the plant far better than the color.

sections.title: A thorny plant
sections.body:
Brambles, the thorny blackberry thickets, turn up in the color books only as plants. Medieval Marian writers used the Song of Solomon image of a lily among brambles to picture the Virgin among maidens [1]. The poet and gardener Derek Jarman lists brambles in autumn among the colors of his garden year [2]. Finlay notes that stylish women had their diamonds reset in platinum, with bramble patterns among the natural motifs [3].

None of these sources describes a bramble color, so the origin of this name as a swatch is undocumented. The dark purple here is a modern name, near [[black]] and [[indigo]], and close to [[cannon]] in darkness.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: As a painted color, bramble is moderately common. It appears in 0.38% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive (90 paintings, as photographed), more often than 52% of the named colors [4]. It peaks in the 1900s, at 2.6 times the rate expected from the museums' own baseline [4].

origin.source: Pastoureau, White, p. 88; Jarman, Chroma, p. 39

notes.cite: ColorHub archive, 23,781 museum paintings as photographed (data/graph/fieldnotes, CIEDE2000)
